title: Stories that disagree
hook: Zhuangzi sings at a death, Seneca endures, Julian sees love in all: different teachings, left in their own houses
tomorrow: the story you'd tell a child

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thoreau, to live deliberately. Your line was deliberately. What did you do on purpose, start to finish? Day ninety-two.

This is the last week of the stories. For seventy days we've sat with Stoics and Zen masters, Nasruddin and Aesop, rabbis and Sufis and desert monks, the Buddha, Confucius, the Gurus, the Gospels and a few ordinary saints. If you've been listening closely, you may have noticed something slightly uncomfortable. They don't all say the same thing. Sometimes they flatly disagree. And there's a temptation, on a path like this one, to smooth that over and pretend it's all one big message. We're not going to do that. Today's story is stories that disagree.
screen: `SEVENTY DAYS OF STORIES.` → `THEY DON'T ALL SAY THE SAME.` → `NO SMOOTHING IT OVER.`

segments.voice: Take three people facing death and loss. First, Zhuangzi, from our Taoist week. When his wife died, a friend found him sitting on the ground, drumming on a pot and singing. Zhuangzi said he had grieved, of course. But then he saw that her life had come out of the great changes of the world, like the seasons turning, and was going back into them. To keep wailing, he said, would be to misunderstand. Second, Seneca, from our Roman nights. Ordered to die by the emperor Nero, he stayed calm, comforted his weeping friends, and said he left them the image of his life. For the Stoics, the thing to do with hardship is to meet it with reason and a steady will; what matters is how you act, and that no one can take away. Third, Julian of Norwich, from last week. In her visions, she saw that everything is held in the love of God. And she heard, in Grace Warrack's translation: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Now listen to how different those are. For Zhuangzi, underneath everything is the turning of nature, and you flow with it. For Seneca, underneath is reason, and you stand firm in it. For Julian, underneath is a loving God who holds it all. Those aren't three ways of saying one thing. They are three different pictures of what the world is. People have held each one, and lived and died well by it. So this path does something simple: it leaves each teaching in its own house, with its own people, in its own words. You can visit all three. You don't have to make them agree, and neither do they.
screen: `ZHUANGZI DRUMS ON THE POT.` · `SENECA STANDS FIRM.` · `JULIAN: ALL SHALL BE WELL.` · `THREE PICTURES, THREE HOUSES.` · then, large: `THEY DON'T HAVE TO AGREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name two stories that pull opposite ways. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the stories that stayed with you. Maybe the ant who stored for winter, and Diogenes who threw away his last cup. Maybe the man who said maybe about his luck, and the Buddha saying pull the arrow now. Find two that tug in different directions. Hold one in each hand. Don't decide between them. Just notice that both have something true in them for you, and that you can carry both. The bell holds the time.
Zhuangzi, drumming on a pot after his wife died: one of three different pictures of what the world is, each left in its own house. Today's word.
Your line: they don't have to agree. Today, when two good pieces of advice pull opposite ways, let them both stand for a while before you choose. Day ninety-two.

howItsDone: Scholars of comparative religion and philosophy try to describe each tradition in its own terms before comparing, and many people on their own path read several traditions side by side without merging them.

myth: Zhuangzi, Seneca and Julian are saying the same thing
they give three different pictures: nature's turning, reason's firmness, God's love.
Zhuangzi said he had grieved before he sang
then he saw her life returning into the great changes, like the seasons.
this path blends traditions into one teaching
it names each source and leaves each teaching in its own house.

fork.setup: you've heard three teachings on death that don't agree. a friend says: just combine them into one. what does this path do?
options: leave each in its own house, and visit all three
fork.reveal: it leaves each in its own house, named and in its own words. you can visit them all; they don't have to agree.

trapdoor: what you thought: all the wisdom traditions are secretly saying one thing.
what it means: they sometimes disagree, and each deserves to be heard in its own terms.
what a scholar hears: Zhuangzi 18, Tacitus on Seneca (Annals 15.62), and Julian's Long Text, chapter 27.
